pull.title: KAFKA-21316: Reuse nodes in PartitionStates to avoid retaining removed entries
pull.body:
PartitionStates keeps its order in a LinkedHashMap and moves a partition
to the end with remove + put. HashMap.removeNode does not clear the next
field of the removed entry, so when two partitions of the same bucket
are updated in turn, every removed entry points at the entry created
after it. Once one of them is promoted to the old generation, young GC
treats it as live and copies every removed entry that follows it, and
the chain keeps growing for as long as both partitions receive data.

We hit this on a follower broker (JDK 21, G1, 16 GiB heap). A mixed GC
ran out of free regions (`Survivor regions: 1->0(0)`) and promoted the
fetcher's entries. Young GC pauses then went from 11 ms to 34 ms on
average and stayed there until restart. A heap dump taken 14 hours later
held 2,048,712 removed `LinkedHashMap$Entry` objects alternating between
the two partitions of one bucket of one fetcher's map.

The only condition is two partitions that keep receiving data, fetched
by the same fetcher thread, whose keys fall into the same bucket of that
fetcher's map. The remove + put has been there since KIP-74. Because the
removed entries form a linked list, one GC worker copies them one by one.
Without a broker, updating two such partitions in turn one million times
leaves 2,000,002 entries reachable from the first removed entry.

This change keeps the order in a doubly linked list of nodes looked up
through a HashMap, and moves the existing node to the end instead of
creating a new one. The leader side does the same rotation for fetch
sessions with ImplicitLinkedHashCollection, which also reuses the
element. `LinkedHashMap.putLast` would do this in one call but needs
Java 21, and clients still targets Java 11.

Behavior is unchanged: order, `partitionStateMap()` as a live
unmodifiable view, and `size()`. `stateIterator()` no longer supports
`remove()`. No caller uses it, and with the old code it left `size()`
stale.

Testing:
- New tests in PartitionStatesTest: an update reuses the entry (fails
  on the old code), and the map view is ordered, live and unmodifiable.
- PartitionStatesTest, SubscriptionStateTest, AbstractFetcherThreadTest,
  ReplicaFetcherThreadTest and ReplicaAlterLogDirsThreadTest pass.
- A randomized comparison against the old class (200,000 mixed
  operations, 5 seeds) observed the same order, values and sizes.

New PartitionStatesBenchmark (JDK 21, `-prof gc`, ns/op and B/op):

```
                        old            new
updateAndMoveToEnd 22   11.6 ns, 40 B   8.6 ns, 0 B
updateAndMoveToEnd 125  11.7 ns, 40 B   5.5 ns, 0 B
updateAndMoveToEnd 1000 13.3 ns, 40 B   6.5 ns, 0 B
stateValue 22            2.1 ns         2.3 ns
stateValue 1000          1.7 ns         2.0 ns
forEach 22              17.9 ns        13.2 ns
forEach 1000            1606 ns        1447 ns
```

ReplicaFetcherThreadBenchmark, `testFetcher` (ns/op):

```
partitions  old              new
100         3,142 +- 490     2,650 +- 34
500         17,843 +- 541    12,900 +- 31
1000        38,029 +- 2,148  32,881 +- 276
5000        229,724 +- 5,314 234,634 +- 11,217
```

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

issue_comments.body:
I have requested a Jira account and will file the issue and add the
KAFKA- number to the title once it is approved. Until then, some
background that is not part of the commit message.

**How we found it.** On a production follower, young GC pauses went
from 11 ms to 34 ms on average right after a mixed GC with no free
regions (`Survivor regions: 1->0(0)`), and were still there when we
took a heap dump 14 hours later. The dump is summarized in the
description.

**Reproduction on brokers.** On three test clusters (JDK 21, G1, heaps
of 1, 2 and 6 GiB) we created two topics whose partitions land in the
same bucket of one follower's fetcher map, produced 1,000 records/s to
each, forced a full GC on the follower, and took a heap dump (`-all`)
ten minutes later. Longest chain of removed `LinkedHashMap$Entry`
objects reachable through `next`:

```
cluster   without this change     with this change
1         838 - 339,594 (4 runs)  2 - 3 (4 runs)
2         7,713 / 309,597         3 / 3
3         2,820 / 2,868           4 / 4
```

With no pair in a shared bucket, the same check gave 34.

**Other tests.** On top of the tests listed in the description, we ran
all `clients` unit tests (13,134), the consumer integration tests (375)
and `kafka.server.*` in core (1,998) with this change. Two tests failed
once each (`KafkaProducerTest.negativePartitionShouldThrow`,
`PlaintextConsumerTest.testAsyncConsumerEndOffsets`) and passed on
three reruns each. The second also passed three runs without this
change.

@chia7712 @junrao could you take a look when you have time? This fixes young GC slowdowns on follower brokers: PartitionStates leaves removed LinkedHashMap entries chained through next, and once one of them is promoted, every young GC copies the whole chain. The fix reuses the node instead of remove + put.

I filed https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-21316 and added it to the title. The Jira also has more test results: reproduction on three test clusters with and without the patch (longest chain 838-339,594 before, 2-4 after), wider regression runs, and production numbers.

A label of 'needs-attention' was automatically added to this PR in order to raise the
attention of the committers. Once this issue has been triaged, the `triage` label
should be removed to prevent this automation from happening again.

commit.message:
Reuse nodes when moving a partition to the end in PartitionStates

PartitionStates kept its order in a LinkedHashMap and moved a partition
to the end with remove + put. HashMap.removeNode does not clear the next
field of the removed entry, so when two partitions of the same bucket
are updated in turn, every removed entry points at the entry created
after it. Once one of them is promoted to the old generation, young GC
treats it as live and copies every removed entry that follows it, and
the chain keeps growing for as long as both partitions receive data.

Keep the order in a doubly linked list of nodes looked up through a
HashMap instead, and move the existing node to the end. Updates no
longer allocate and no removed entry is left behind.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
